title: Infrastructure Failure Lab
subtitle: Think like the engineer on call. Predict, inspect evidence, decide, and defend your proof.
disclosure: Recorded incident snapshots and design exercises only. This browser is an offline training simulator; it does not execute commands, reach AWS, inspect your laptop, or persist your answers.

missions.title: Running VM. No disk. No IP.
missions.story: Terraform reports a running domain. There is no DHCP lease, SSH cannot connect, and the guest drops to initramfs. Take the role of the on-call engineer before touching the network.

evidence.label: Host signals · recorded
evidence.body:
libvirt domain: running
DHCP leases on default network: none
Host disk mapping: vda -> tfaws-lab01-root.qcow2
Guest console: initramfs rescue shell

evidence.label: Guest boot · recorded
evidence.body:
ALERT! LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs does not exist
/proc/partitions: only sr0 (cloud-init ISO)
/sys/block: sr0 and loop devices; no vda
VirtIO PCI 0000:03:00.0 (0x1042): NO DRIVER
virtio-pci: Unable to change power state from D3cold to D0

phases.question: The domain is 'running', but it has no lease. What is the best next observation?
choices: Restart dnsmasq and reconfigure the host bridge
Open the guest serial console and check its boot state
Replace the Ubuntu qcow2 image
phases.why: A running QEMU process only proves the virtual machine process is alive. It does not prove the guest kernel booted or reached DHCP. The serial console reveals the earlier failure without altering host networking.
phases.hint: Which observation lets you distinguish a boot failure from a networking failure?
phases.proof: The actual guest console revealed the initramfs error before any DHCP request.

phases.question: Why is changing root=LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs the wrong first fix?
choices: The kernel sees no virtio root block device at all; investigate PCI/device binding first
cloud-init always rewrites disk labels on first boot
dnsmasq must assign an IP before Linux can mount its root disk
phases.why: The guest can see sr0 but not vda. A wrong filesystem label would still leave a visible block device. The missing device, PCI VirtIO IDs and D3cold errors point to virtual PCI device accessibility/binding.
phases.hint: Can a filesystem label be queried on a disk the kernel cannot see?
phases.proof: Only sr0 appeared in /proc/partitions even after modprobe; VirtIO devices were present in PCI without drivers.

phases.question: Which proposed remediation preserves data and matches the observed outcome on this host?
choices: Disable AppArmor and recreate the entire storage pool
Change machine type q35 to pc, review a VM-only plan, then verify guest boot
Conclude that q35 never supports Ubuntu or VirtIO
phases.why: On this particular host, switching q35 PCIe topology to the pc/i440fx machine yielded working VirtIO disks and networking. Terraform planned 0 adds, 1 in-place VM change, 0 destroys. This is not a universal q35 rule.
phases.hint: Look for the smallest change supported by the evidence and check the Terraform plan.
phases.proof: Post-change guest obtained 192.168.122.230, completed cloud-init, and the final Terraform plan showed No changes.

missions.debrief: Reliability is layered: a running hypervisor process is not OS readiness. Diagnose from the guest console, then require a narrow plan and independent post-change evidence.

missions.title: QEMU fails before boot
missions.story: QEMU refuses to start because its confinement policy does not permit opening files in the qcow2 backing chain, then the cloud-init ISO. The easiest workaround would also weaken host security.

evidence.label: QEMU / host · incident summary
evidence.body:
Root disk: sparse qcow2 overlay
Backing image: Ubuntu cloud-image qcow2
AppArmor: file access denied on backing image
After root fix: access denied on cloud-init ISO
Both originally referenced through source.volume

evidence.label: Repository mitigation · source-derived
evidence.body:
domain.devices.disks[0].source.file = libvirt_volume.root.path
domain.devices.disks[1].source.file = libvirt_volume.seed.path
Existing libvirt storage pool and AppArmor remain enabled

phases.question: The VM cannot start even though both volumes exist. What evidence best narrows the failure?
choices: Inspect QEMU/libvirt startup logs and AppArmor denials
Change DHCP range until a lease appears
SSH to devops inside the unbooted VM
phases.why: A startup denial precedes guest execution. Host QEMU/libvirt/AppArmor evidence is the right layer. DHCP and SSH cannot be the root cause of a guest that never started.
phases.hint: Where can a process-start failure be observed before the guest OS runs?
phases.proof: The incident revealed denial to a qcow2 backing file and later to the seed ISO.

phases.question: How do you restore access without removing the security boundary?
choices: Disable AppArmor globally
Chmod 777 every image and switch the disk to raw
Use supported direct source.file references for both disk and ISO, then review the plan
phases.why: Referencing the file paths lets libvirt's AppArmor helper discover the image chain on this host; it avoids a global security downgrade. Filesystem permissions alone do not override MAC policy.
phases.hint: Can we change how the hypervisor declares files rather than turn off confinement?
phases.proof: Both disk declarations now use source.file and the guest subsequently booted with AppArmor still active.

phases.question: Which evidence is required before saying the mitigation is complete?
choices: Only that 'terraform validate' passes
Only that the qcow2 file exists
QEMU starts, guest sees the disk, cloud-init completes, and host health request succeeds
phases.why: Static configuration and file existence are necessary but insufficient. Verify across the host, guest, bootstrap and application layers.
phases.hint: A file-access fix is useful only if the guest can now boot and serve traffic.
phases.proof: Real guest: cloud-init done, systemd service active, /health returned JSON status ok, then Terraform showed no drift.

missions.debrief: Prefer narrow policy-compatible fixes over disabling host security. Distinguish hypervisor startup, kernel boot, provisioning and application availability.

missions.title: Someone changed infrastructure manually
missions.story: Someone modifies only the Name tag of the managed VPC outside Terraform using the local Floci API. Terraform is expected to detect drift and restore the intended value — but only after the planned changes are inspected.

evidence.label: Drill contract · source-derived
evidence.body:
Terraform expected Name: terraform-aws-lab-vpc
Out-of-band Name: terraform-aws-lab-out-of-band
Plan -detailed-exitcode: 2 means changes
Guard: exactly one update, only the VPC Name tag
After approved repair: plan exit 0

evidence.label: Safety boundaries
evidence.body:
AWS CLI endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:4566
Disposable test credentials are injected in a child process
Repair requires typing yes
Drill does not touch a real AWS account

phases.question: What does Terraform exit code 2 mean with -detailed-exitcode?
choices: The plan found changes between desired and actual state
The provider credentials are incorrect
Everything is already identical
phases.why: With -detailed-exitcode, exit 0 means no diff, 1 means error, and 2 means a non-empty plan. You still need to inspect WHAT would change.
phases.hint: Compare it with exit 0 after a successful repair.
phases.proof: scripts/drift-lab.sh explicitly requires 2 before it proceeds with its safety gate.

phases.question: The planned repair unexpectedly replaces an EC2 instance too. What should happen?
choices: Apply immediately because Terraform is declarative
Block repair and investigate the unexpected resource changes
Edit the tfstate file by hand to suppress the diff
phases.why: A plan with additional or destructive changes is outside the approved scope. The drill asserts one VPC Name update and compares all other attributes before allowing a repair.
phases.hint: What would an engineer check before making changes to resources outside the ticket?
phases.proof: The script compares the complete before/after object after removing only the permitted Name fields.

phases.question: Which sequence demonstrates idempotent, controlled recovery?
choices: Change tag via AWS CLI, run auto-approve destroy, declare success
Require exact plan scope, ask approval, apply saved plan, verify tag and zero-change plan
Delete local Terraform state and initialize again
phases.why: Reviewing and applying a saved plan with approval prevents an unreviewed replacement. The final plan must show no changes, and the external API must show the restored tag.
phases.hint: The best proof is both Terraform output and an independent API observation.
phases.proof: make local-drift implements the guard, prompts for explicit consent, verifies actual tag and final plan exit 0.

missions.debrief: Terraform is not magic: plan exit codes, state, external API evidence, scope-of-change checks and deliberate approval are separate controls.

missions.title: Green CI — but not real AWS
missions.story: Your tests pass against a local AWS API emulator. A reviewer asks whether that proves the security groups, IAM and routing will behave correctly in real AWS.

evidence.label: Local provider configuration
evidence.body:
access_key = test
secret_key = test
endpoints.ec2/iam/sts = http://127.0.0.1:4566
skip_credentials_validation = true
Floci default: EC2 disabled; no Docker socket mount

evidence.label: Three verification layers
evidence.body:
1. terraform test + mock provider: configuration assertions
2. Floci integration: local emulated API behavior
3. Real AWS sandbox: actual cloud behavior (not exercised by default)

phases.question: Which statement about passing mock tests and Floci integration is defensible?
choices: This proves every real AWS IAM/network behavior
These prove configuration intent and certain local API flows, not production AWS behavior
Green CI guarantees the public cloud has been provisioned
phases.why: Mocked providers are plan-time assertions. Emulated API responses can verify workflows locally but cannot establish real AWS network isolation, IAM enforcement, cost or resiliency.
phases.hint: What actually executed: a real AWS service or a local implementation of selected APIs?
phases.proof: The repository explicitly distinguishes mock tests, Floci emulator integration, and guarded real AWS.

phases.question: Why is Floci EC2 execution intentionally off by default?
choices: Docker's host socket would grant powerful host control to the emulator
EC2 is impossible to model in Terraform
It is safe to expose the Docker socket from any container
phases.why: A mounted /var/run/docker.sock is a privileged host-control boundary. The project avoids that shortcut by default and still exercises network/IAM Terraform code.
phases.hint: What could an untrusted process do with the host Docker daemon?
phases.proof: The README and Compose configuration do not mount the Docker socket and compute is disabled.

phases.question: If you later want to test real AWS, which separation is essential?
choices: Change localhost endpoints to cloud endpoints in the same state root
Reuse emulator test credentials for production
Use the isolated AWS root, expected-account guard, scoped credentials, cost approval and explicit plan
phases.why: The separate roots stop accidental endpoint or state sharing. The AWS wrapper verifies account identity and requires deliberate confirmation. These guards reduce risk but are not a cost guarantee.
phases.hint: Where do state, credentials and provider endpoints need hard boundaries?
phases.proof: environments/aws/provider.tf restricts allowed_account_ids; the guarded wrapper is scripts/aws-command.sh.

missions.debrief: Evidence has a scope. Name the exact system actually exercised. Security includes the privilege you refuse to grant just to make a demo easier.

missions.title: Private EC2 can't reach SSM
missions.story: The Terraform design attaches an SSM IAM instance profile to a private-only EC2 instance. There is no NAT and no SSM VPC endpoints. An engineer assumes Session Manager access will work merely because the role is attached.

evidence.label: Network design · repo source
evidence.body:
VPC CIDR 10.42.0.0/16
Private subnets: 10.42.10.0/24 and 10.42.11.0/24
Private route table: implicit local route ONLY
No NAT gateway, no interface VPC endpoints

evidence.label: Compute / identity defaults
evidence.body:
enable_compute = false (default)
associate_public_ip_address = false
security group: zero inbound; HTTPS egress to VPC CIDR only
IAM role: AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
IMDSv2 required; encrypted root volume

phases.question: Why is SSM access NOT yet proven for this instance?
choices: The role alone is sufficient, even without any network path
The agent needs reachability to SSM service endpoints; the private subnet has no such path
The security group must expose inbound TCP 22
phases.why: IAM authorizes API actions but does not create routes or private service endpoints. The network is isolated, and a management path to AWS SSM services is absent.
phases.hint: Separate identity authorization from network reachability.
phases.proof: Network module omits NAT/endpoints, while the identity module only supplies the SSM policy.

phases.question: What is a secure design direction for private SSM management?
choices: Assign a public IP, allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0, and hardcode keys
Add required private SSM interface endpoints and appropriate endpoint SG/DNS policies, then test
Remove the instance profile because it is unused
phases.why: Interface endpoints can supply private connectivity for SSM services without an internet path. Exact endpoints and security-group rules depend on the supported region, agent version and design; they are not present in this repository.
phases.hint: Can the service be reached privately without public ingress?
phases.proof: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md intentionally lists endpoints as a future extension, not an implemented feature.

phases.question: How should an interview demo state the SSM outcome today?
choices: SSM is production-ready because terraform test is green
The private instance and SSM connectivity are not deployed/proven; explain missing endpoints and a real verification plan
The Floci emulator proves public AWS SSM sessions
phases.why: The compute resource is disabled by default, and Floci does not verify real AWS networking. A credible engineer explicitly names untested claims and designs a constrained verification procedure.
phases.hint: Has a real AWS managed instance registered and accepted a test session?
phases.proof: The optional AWS runbook requires a separate sandbox, account controls and deliberate opt-in.

missions.debrief: Identity, routing, DNS, security groups and endpoints are independent dependencies. A secure design also states what was intentionally left unimplemented.

missions.title: Boot completed. Is the service ready?
missions.story: The guest now boots. Cloud-init provisions a locked-password devops user, installs a Python HTTP service and starts it via systemd. You need to prove the delivered function works from both guest and host.

evidence.label: Real guest verification · recorded
evidence.body:
Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS on tfaws-lab01
cloud-init status → done
systemctl is-active lab-health → active
curl http://localhost:8080/health → {"status":"ok","service":"terraform-libvirt-lab"}

evidence.label: Real host verification · recorded
evidence.body:
devops SSH using dedicated ed25519 key succeeded
IP assigned by libvirt DHCP: 192.168.122.230
curl from host to guest:8080/health → status ok
Terraform plan → No changes

phases.question: The serial console asks for a login/password. How was this lab designed to authenticate?
choices: Root password is stored in terraform.tfstate for console login
The devops account uses a dedicated SSH public key; password login is disabled
Any guest can log in without credentials because this is local KVM
phases.why: cloud-init config disables root login/password SSH and locks the devops password; it injects only the public half of a dedicated key. The private half stays on the reviewer host.
phases.hint: Read ssh_pwauth, lock_passwd and ssh_authorized_keys in the template.
phases.proof: The guest's authorized_keys contained the dedicated lab key; SSH login as devops succeeded.

phases.question: What is stronger proof than just 'the VM is running'?
choices: Only checking that /dev/vda is present
Cloud-init done, systemd active, and HTTP /health returns expected JSON from the host
Terraform fmt succeeds without booting a VM
phases.why: The end-to-end request validates the provisioning pipeline and network path to the application, while cloud-init and systemd expose independent boot/setup and process signals.
phases.hint: Can a running hypervisor tell you whether your actual API is serving?
phases.proof: Both guest and host returned {"status":"ok","service":"terraform-libvirt-lab"}.

phases.question: Does this /health success prove the whole design is production hardened?
choices: Yes, HTTP 200 proves durability, authentication and recovery
No, it proves this small API and path; security, persistence, fault-tolerance and load testing are separate
Yes, systemd automatically encrypts every network request
phases.why: This endpoint is intentionally minimal, unauthenticated and binds to 0.0.0.0 inside the NAT guest. It is an educational reachability check, not a protected production API or availability SLO.
phases.hint: What does the handler actually test beyond returning a fixed JSON body?
phases.proof: The Python HTTP handler only responds to GET /health with a constant JSON response.

missions.debrief: A successful deployment needs evidence across identity, boot, service manager, application and network. A health endpoint proves exactly what it checks — no more.

missions.title: Which green badge can you trust?
missions.story: Two GitHub Actions jobs fail while KVM is already functional locally. After a formatting-only commit, all five project CI jobs pass. A reviewer asks what this does and does not establish.

evidence.label: Initial failed CI · recorded
evidence.body:
Terraform format / validation / mock tests: failure
Local Linux VM / Terraform validation: failure
Log: terraform fmt -check -recursive
Found: environments/libvirt/main.tf
Cause: indentation/alignment; exit 3

evidence.label: After style-only commit · recorded
evidence.body:
Terraform format / validation / mock tests: success
Local Linux VM / Terraform validation: success
Floci AWS API integration: success
Trivy IaC security scan: success
Gitleaks secret scan: success
KVM runtime verified independently on laptop

phases.question: Both format-related jobs fail, but the VM runs locally. What is the accurate incident classification?
choices: The VM runtime is definitely broken
CI formatting gate failed; inspect logs before claiming Terraform validation failed too
Trivy proves that formatting is optional
phases.why: A job can fail at its first command and skip subsequent validation. A formatting failure does not imply a runtime fault. The exact failed step is the evidence.
phases.hint: A red job doesn't tell you which step failed; open its log.
phases.proof: Both jobs exited on terraform fmt -check before reaching their remaining steps.

phases.question: All five CI checks now pass. What still needs separate evidence?
choices: Actual KVM guest boot, SSH, cloud-init and host-to-guest HTTP behavior
Whether the HCL parses
Whether secrets were committed to the repository
phases.why: The GitHub runner doesn't create the actual laptop KVM guest. It verifies static Terraform, mocked/emulated interactions and scanners; physical runtime validation is independent.
phases.hint: Where did the VM with 192.168.122.230 actually run?
phases.proof: The laptop console, SSH session and curl demonstrated runtime, and a subsequent Terraform plan showed no drift.

phases.question: What is the strongest honest portfolio claim?
choices: One passing Actions page proves AWS production readiness
The repository contains tested HCL, emulated API checks and a real KVM runtime demo; AWS production behavior is explicitly untested
The VPC IAM policy means real EC2 was deployed automatically
phases.why: Good engineering distinguishes configuration tests, emulator behavior and actual guest runtime, while listing unverified cloud behavior and future endpoints/cost constraints.
phases.hint: Name what was exercised, where it ran, and which guarantees remain out of scope.
phases.proof: Inspect five checks in CI, the local VM runbook, and the security model's 'does not prove' column.

missions.debrief: A good engineering demo is falsifiable: show exact checks, distinguish CI evidence from runtime evidence, and explicitly state what is still unknown.
